o: A client sending forged cookies to the server
Making the server send HTTP requests to destinations chosen by the attacker
Forging server-side certificates to intercept TLS traffic
Injecting malicious SQL through a server-side API
questions.x: SSRF exploits a server feature that fetches a URL. The attacker controls the target URL, causing the server to make requests from its own network to internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, or other restricted targets.
questions.h: The S in SSRF stands for Server-Side. The R stands for Request. The F stands for Forgery. Who is forging what request on behalf of whom?

questions.q: Why is SSRF particularly dangerous in cloud environments?
o: Cloud servers run slower, giving attackers more time
Cloud metadata services at 169.254.169.254 return IAM credentials when requested from within the instance, making SSRF a path to cloud account compromise
Cloud servers cannot apply URL filters
TLS is disabled by default in cloud networks
questions.x: AWS, GCP, and Azure expose instance metadata at a link-local address only reachable from within the VM. An SSRF to that address can return credentials that give the attacker full control of the cloud account.
questions.h: What special address is only accessible from within a cloud instance and returns credentials? Think about the AWS metadata service.

questions.q: What is the difference between blind SSRF and non-blind SSRF?
o: Blind SSRF only targets localhost, non-blind targets internal networks
In blind SSRF, the server fetches the URL but the response is not returned to the attacker, in non-blind, the attacker sees the response
Blind SSRF uses POST requests, non-blind uses GET
Blind SSRF requires authentication, non-blind does not
questions.x: Non-blind SSRF lets you read internal service responses directly. Blind SSRF still causes the server to make the request, but you infer success via out-of-band methods: DNS callbacks, timing differences, or error messages.
questions.h: Blind means you cannot directly see the result. How would you know the SSRF worked if the response stays on the server?

questions.q: Which of these is a common internal target for SSRF attacks in web applications?
o: https://google.com
http://localhost:6379 (Redis) or http://192.168.x.x:8080/admin
https://cdn.cloudflare.com
The application's own public domain
questions.x: Redis at localhost:6379, internal admin panels at 192.168.x.x, Kubernetes API servers, and cloud metadata services are all common SSRF targets. They are accessible from the server's network but not from the public internet.
questions.h: The value of SSRF comes from reaching things that are not publicly accessible. What types of services exist on the internal network of a typical web server?

questions.q: What is an allowlist-based URL filter and why is it more secure than a blocklist?
o: An allowlist requires HTTPS, while a blocklist blocks HTTP. HTTPS is inherently more secure
An allowlist explicitly permits only approved domains or IP ranges, a blocklist tries to block known bad addresses, which attackers can bypass with redirects or encoding tricks
An allowlist is client-side, a blocklist is server-side
They offer the same security, the choice is stylistic
questions.x: Blocklists fail when attackers use open redirects, decimal IP notation, IPv6 addresses, or DNS rebinding to bypass specific blocked patterns. An allowlist rejects anything not explicitly approved, making bypasses much harder.
questions.h: Blocklists try to enumerate all bad inputs. Allowlists enumerate all good inputs. Which is harder to enumerate completely?
